mercy_translation.text:
This great work was truly fitting above all to the goodness of God.

For if a king who has built a house or a city does not simply ignore it when, through the negligence of its inhabitants, it is attacked by robbers, but avenges and preserves it as his own work—looking not at the negligence of those who live there but at what is fitting to himself—how much more did the Word of the all-good Father not overlook the human race, made through him, as it descended into corruption. Rather, through the offering of his own body he wiped away the death that had occurred, corrected their negligence by his teaching, and set right all human affairs by his own power.

One may be assured of these things from the writings of the Savior's own inspired theologians, where they say: “For the love of Christ constrains us, having judged this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that we might no longer live for ourselves but for him who died and rose again from the dead for us,” our Lord Jesus Christ. And again: “We see Jesus, who for a little while was made lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death on behalf of everyone.”

Then Scripture also indicates why it was necessary that none other than God the Word himself should become man, saying: “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, to perfect through sufferings the pioneer of their salvation.” By saying this it indicates that it belonged to none other to bring human beings back from the corruption that had occurred except the Word of God, who had also made them in the beginning.

And that the Word himself took a body for the sacrifice on behalf of bodies like ours is also indicated when they say: “Since therefore the children have shared in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might abolish the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their whole life.”

For through the sacrifice of his own body he both brought to an end the law that stood against us and renewed for us a beginning of life by giving the hope of resurrection. Since through human beings death had gained power over human beings, for this reason again through the Word of God's becoming man there came the destruction of death and the resurrection of life, as the Christ-bearing man says: “Since through a human being came death, through a human being also came the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive,” and what follows.

For now we no longer die as those condemned, but as those who are to rise we await the common resurrection of all, which “in its own times” God—who has accomplished and given it—will reveal.

This, then, is the first cause of the Savior's becoming man. From what follows one may also know that his gracious coming among us took place reasonably and fittingly.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The biblical quotations are translated from the form in Athanasius' Greek text.
Athanasius calls this the 'first cause' of the Incarnation: the defeat of death and corruption through the Word's embodied self-offering.
